analysis.one_liner: Ends civil asset forfeiture, letting government take property only after conviction or a full criminal-style trial.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a single cosponsor, never getting a hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Civil asset forfeiture lets police take a person's cash, car, or home without ever charging them with a crime, because the lawsuit is technically filed against the property itself. This bill would shut that down at the federal level entirely, and in the states would allow civil seizure only after a criminal conviction, or after the state proved its case in a proceeding where the owner got the same rights as criminal defendants, including a lawyer and a jury trial. It also created a federal court option for people whose property states took improperly.
analysis.who_benefits: Property owners who would otherwise have to sue to get their own money or homes back, especially people with modest means who cannot afford a lawyer to fight a seizure. Innocent people whose cars, cash, or houses get swept up because someone else used them also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits all federal civil asset forfeiture, including nonjudicial administrative forfeiture, so no one loses property to the federal government without a criminal case.

Bars states from taking a person's property through civil forfeiture unless the owner was criminally convicted, or the state proved the offense in a proceeding where the owner had criminal-defendant constitutional rights, including counsel and a jury trial.
Creates a federal cause of action letting people sue a state in federal court to get back property forfeited in violation of those limits.

Keeps criminal forfeiture in place, so property can still be taken from people actually convicted of a crime, while adding counsel for indigent owners and a rebuttable presumption favoring innocent third parties in related proceedings.

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state law enforcement agencies, which currently keep the proceeds of property they seize, would lose that revenue stream, and prosecutors would have to prove crimes before taking property.

drawbacks.text: Law enforcement and prosecutors argue civil forfeiture is a key tool for dismantling drug trafficking rings and recovering crime proceeds, particularly when the property owner is absent or unidentifiable, a problem this bill would leave harder to solve at the state level.

The bill's restrictions on state forfeiture rest on a sweeping reading of Congress's power over the states (Title II, Section 202), which state governments and some courts would likely challenge as federal overreach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real but narrow: criminal forfeiture after conviction remains available, so convicted drug traffickers can still lose their assets. What disappears is the ability to take property from people never convicted of anything, whose burden falls most heavily on low-income owners who cannot afford a legal fight. The main design risk is the untested constitutional basis for the state-level provision.

outcome.mechanism: A single member introduced it in the last weeks of the session, no one else signed on, the committees never took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Justin Amash (I-MI) introduced the bill on December 17, 2020, seventeen days before the 116th Congress ended.
The bill had zero cosponsors, from either party.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction; neither committee took any further action on it.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or any further action of any kind occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies that collect and keep forfeiture proceeds are better off, since the tool stayed fully available. No hearing or debate ever happened, so the property-rights argument it raised never got an official airing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies that keep seizures

for.name: Justin Amash
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill on the House floor with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never acted on the provisions within its jurisdiction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew support or opposition from either party: its only sponsor was an Independent former Republican, and the record shows zero cosponsors and no votes.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Agencies can currently keep cash, vehicles, and homes seized through civil forfeiture, and many use those proceeds for operations and equipment, often without a criminal conviction. The bill would cut off that revenue unless they first win a criminal case, which is why their interest in the bill runs against the property owners it protects.

Civil forfeiture lets prosecutors pursue property without the burden of proving a defendant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The bill would require conviction or a full trial with criminal-defendant rights, removing that shortcut.
